'''''Phyllostachys bambusoides''''', commonly called '''{{not a typo|madake}}''', '''giant timber bamboo''', or '''Japanese timber bamboo''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Bambusoideae|bamboo]] subfamily of the grass family [[Poaceae]], native to China, and possibly also to Japan.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book | editor-last = Brickell | editor-first = Christopher | title = The Royal Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants | year = 2008 | page = 811 | publisher = Dorling Kindersley | location = United Kingdom | isbn = 9781405332965}}</ref>

==Description==
''Phyllostachys bambusoides'' is a "running" (monopodial type) evergreen bamboo<ref name=RHSAZ/> which can reach a height of roughly {{cvt|20|m}} and a diameter of {{cvt|10|cm}}. The [[Culm (botany)|culms]] are dark green, with a thin wall that thickens with maturity, and very straight, with long internodes and two distinctive rings at the node.<ref name="bamboo in japan">{{cite book |last1=Bess |first1=Nancy Moore |last2=Wein |first2=Bibi |title=bamboo in japan |date=2001 |publisher=Kodansha International |location=New York |page=34 |edition=1st}}</ref> The species is thin-skinned, easily split lengthwise, has long fibres, and is strong and highly flexible, even when split finely.<ref name="bamboo in japan"/>

Leaves are dark green, and the sheaths are strong and hairless. New stalks emerge in late spring and grow at a rate of up to {{cvt|1|m}} a day; one specimen produced culms growing a remarkable {{cvt|120|cm}} in 24 hours.<ref>Robert Austin and Koichiro Ueda, BAMBOO (New York: Walker/Weatherhill, 1970) p. 193.</ref> The flowering interval of this species is very long, lasting roughly 120 years.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Carl |last1=Veller |first2=Martin A. |last2=Nowak |authorlink2=Martin Nowak |first3=Charles C. |last3=Davis |title=Letter: Extended flowering intervals of bamboos evolved by discrete multiplication |date=July 2015 |volume=18 |issue=7 |journal=[[Ecology Letters]] |pages=653–659 |doi=10.1111/ele.12442 |pmid=25963600 |issn=1461-023X |accessdate=April 1, 2016 |url-status=dead |url=http://www.people.fas.harvard.edu/~ccdavis/pdfs/Veller_et_al_Ecology_Letters_2015.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150911202926/http://www.people.fas.harvard.edu/~ccdavis/pdfs/Veller_et_al_Ecology_Letters_2015.pdf |archive-date=2015-09-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title= Bamboo Mathematicians |author= Carl Zimmer |authorlink= Carl Zimmer |date= May 15, 2015 |publisher= [[National Geographic Society|National Geographic]] |url= http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2015/05/15/bamboo-mathematicians/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150517210059/http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2015/05/15/bamboo-mathematicians/ |url-status= dead |archive-date= May 17, 2015 |accessdate= April 1, 2016}}</ref>

==Uses==
In Asia, ''Phyllostachys bambusoides'', known in [[Japan]] as {{transliteration|ja|madake}}, is one of the preferred bamboos for construction and furniture manufacture.{{citation needed|date=April 2016}} Its properties also make it useful in a number of traditional Japanese arts and crafts:
* Both {{transliteration|ja|madake}} and ''[[Phyllostachys edulis]]'' (known in [[Japanese language|Japanese]] as {{transliteration|ja|moso}}) are used in the making of {{transliteration|ja|[[shakuhachi]]}} flutes<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://yungflutes.com/guide/faq/what_is_madake_bamboo/|title=What is madake bamboo?|last=Yung|first=Perry|date=2009|website=www.yungflutes.com}}</ref><ref name="bamboo in japan"/>
* The hairless and flexible sheaths of {{transliteration|ja|madake}} - known as {{transliteration|ja|takekawa}} or {{transliteration|ja|takenokawa}} - make it apt for wrapping food, and in the production of {{transliteration|ja|[[Baren (printing tool)|baren]]}} woodblock printing tools.
* The uniform, plain-colour sheaths of the variety {{transliteration|ja|kashirodake}} were traditionally used to weave the coverings of some [[Geta (footwear)|geta]], a covering known as {{transliteration|ja|tatami omote}}; however, in modern times, the variety used is a different and unknown species, grown in China and bleached to be plain in colour.<ref>{{cite web |title=雪駄(雪踏)についての考察〜その24: 雪駄表の製造工程 |url=http://settajyuku2.blog.fc2.com/blog-entry-78.html |website=魁!!雪駄塾 SAKIGAKE!!SETTA JYUKU |access-date=21 August 2019}}</ref>
* The long internodes and equally long fibres of the bamboo make it ideal for traditional [[Japanese bamboo weaving|basket-weaving]] and the production of [[Hand fan#Japan|fans]].

Historically, madake was used to create relatively durable carbon filaments in early [[incandescent light bulb]]s. The [[Thomas_Edison#Electric_light_company|Edison Electric Light Company]] used madake from [[Yawata]] for about fifteen years.<ref name=Morris>{{cite book|author=[[Edmund Morris (writer)|Edmund Morris]]|title=Edison|year=2019|isbn=9780812983210|lccn=2019005173|page=394}}</ref>

[[File:Thomas Edison Monument at Yawata.jpg|thumb|alt=Edison Monument in Yawata|A monument to [[Thomas Edison]] at the [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū]] shrine near the madake groves in [[Yawata]].]]

''Phyllostachys bambusoides'' is cultivated as an ornamental plant in temperate zones worldwide, with numerous [[cultivar]]s being available. Some grow to extreme lengths and heights, making them typically only suitable for parks and large gardens; however, more compact cultivars are available.

The following cultivars are recipients of the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:<ref>{{cite web

| page = 78 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 26 April 2018}}</ref>
* 'Castillonii'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/86716/i-Phyllostachys-bambusoides-i-Castillonii/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Phyllostachys bambusoides'' 'Castillonii' | access-date = 25 April 2018}}</ref> – yellow canes, {{cvt|4.5|m|ft}}
* 'Holochrysa'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/103786/i-Phyllostachys-bambusoides-i-Holochrysa/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Phyllostachys bambusoides'' 'Holochrysa' | access-date = 25 April 2018}}</ref> – rich yellow canes, {{cvt|8|m|ft}}
